moves.spoken: White grabs the centre, and Black fianchettoes with g6 — the King's Indian again.
White chooses the Fianchetto Variation, and Black completes the kingside setup — the bishop to g7 and castling.
Development, and Black holds back with d6.
White develops the knight to f3. Now, where does Black's queen's knight belong — c6 or d7? At a high level, the knight to c6 can backfire.
The reason: the knight to c6 invites the annoying d5. So the knight to d7 is the typical choice — safe, and preparing e5.
And there it is, e5 — with the knight on d7, that break is well supported.
White builds with e4. And yes, what about that bishop on c8? It will get out in due course.
Here is an interesting idea: c6, controlling the d5 square — and it also prepares the queen to a5.
The queen swings to a5 — this is the main line, leaning on the c4-pawn.
At the right moment Black strikes with the capture on d4, and White recaptures with the knight.
And now the knight jumps into e5 — hyper-modern chess in action: White holds more of the centre, but Black's pieces swarm it, and this one leans on the c4-pawn.
White retreats the bishop to f1 to defend. But look — both White pawns are under fire from Black's pieces, and the whole battle turns on whether White can beat back the initiative.
Black brings the rook to e8, ramping up the pressure on the e-pawn and tempting White into f4.

White tucks the king to h2. Now, that knight on d4 is very active — can Black force it to move while piling on the e-pawn and developing at the same time? Note that c5 would be a mistake, badly weakening the d5 square; a subtler method is wanted.

And there it is — the queen to c5, a really clever move, x-raying f2. The threat is the capture on d4 and then a knight to f3. Here is the tell: when White has played g3 but the bishop has left the fianchetto, the f3 square becomes a tactical hot-spot — let your tactical metal detector start beeping.
White scrambles the knight to a4, but he is in deep trouble.
And the queen takes on d4 — winning the knight, and the game is over.
In review, the queen to a5 is genuinely the main line here, hitting the c4-pawn — a line worth practising, and one played for years at the top.
